title: Living ashtpadi 24
hookLine: the psalm ends where it began: peace in remembering

cards: A round is a song that chases itself. One voice starts, a second joins a line later, then a third, and the tune keeps circling back to its own beginning. Children learn them at camp around a fire.

The fun is that there's no real ending: when you reach the last line, you're already back at the first. Sukhmani is long, twenty-four ashtpadis. But when you reach the last one, you find you've come back around.

teach.h: THE LAST ASHTPADI: PERFECT, BREATH BY BREATH.
teach.b: Here's the twenty-fourth ashtpadi in brief. Its salok rings pooraa four times: the perfect Lord, perfect Name, perfect One found and praised.

Its first stanza calls us to the perfect Guru's teaching and to remember God with every breath, so the mind's anxiety lifts. And over it all hangs Sukhmani's center line: the jewel of peace is the ambrosial Name.
Now go back to the very first stanza of Sukhmani.

teach.h: SIMRAU SIMAR SIMAR: THE FIRST LINE.
teach.b: It opens with a run of one word: simrau simar simar sukh paavau. In paraphrase: I remember, remembering, remembering, I find peace, and the troubles of the body are erased. Simran: remembering, keeping God in mind.
And sukh: peace. That's the first line.

teach.h: THE SAME TWO THINGS AT THE END.
teach.b: Twenty-four ashtpadis later, the bani closes on the same two things: the Name, remembered, and the peace it brings. Why does that matter? A circle tells you something a straight line doesn't.
A straight line says: finish this, and you're done.
A circle says: this is a path you walk again. Sukhmani isn't read once and filed away. Some Sikhs recite it daily, some weekly, and some gather to recite it together.
Each time, the first line and the last line meet. Living the twenty-fourth ashtpadi isn't reaching a finish.
It's coming back around to remembering, and finding the peace was waiting there the whole time.

how: Sukhmani Sahib opens with simran bringing peace and closes on the same Name, and Sikhs recite it daily or weekly, alone or together, returning to that circle.

o: a memory test of hymns learned by heart
a long prayer read once, start to finish
remembering God, keeping the Name in mind

s: Sukhmani's first line is about remembering and peace
simrau simar simar sukh paavau: remembering, I find peace.
Sukhmani is meant to be read once and filed away
Sikhs recite it again and again, daily or weekly, alone or together.
Sukhmani ends on a theme it never mentioned before
it ends where it began: the Name remembered, and peace.

games.q: you finish the twenty-fourth ashtpadi. by today's lesson, what have you reached?
o: the end; you're done for good.
the beginning again: remembering, and peace.
games.why: Sukhmani is a circle: it opens with simran bringing sukh, and closes on the same Name and peace.

practice: For the first minute, remember gently, someone who loves you, a time you felt held, a moment of beauty; if you pray, remember God and let Waheguru come with the breath, like Sukhmani's first line, remembering, remembering.
For the second minute, stop remembering and simply rest in whatever peace it left behind.

wordCard.voice: Simran, remembering God: Sukhmani opens with simran bringing sukh, remembering bringing peace, and closes on the same Name and the same peace.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering God; Sukhmani's first line repeats simar, remember.

carryVoice: Your line: peace in remembering. The first line and the last, holding hands. Same time tomorrow.
